title: Mid-term: sorting, functions, objects and brute force
overview: The mid-term mixes the first modules: return a sorted heap array from a function, sort characters inside lines read until end of input, pick the best student with a tie rule, and brute-force a three-sum check. Two solutions are logically fine but use too much stack memory and crash on Windows - a good lesson in where big arrays belong.

concepts.explain: A function can `new` an array, fill it and return the pointer; the caller deletes it.
Either `sort(..., greater<int>())` or print an ascending array backwards.
`sort(p + l, p + r)` sorts only indices `l..r-1`.
Compare the main key first, and only when equal compare the second key.
Try all combinations; fine when N is small (N=100 gives about 10^6 triples).
Big local arrays can overflow the stack; make them global, `static`, or heap-allocated.

files.title: Sort It (simple version)
files.what: Reads an array, sorts it ascending and prints it, then sorts it descending and prints it again.
steps: Read `n` and `a`.
`sort(a, a+n)` then print.
`sort(a, a+n, greater<int>())` then print.
files.input_note: First line N, then N numbers.

check.q: Could you print the descending line without sorting again?
check.a: Yes - print the ascending array from the last index to the first.

files.title: Sort It (function + heap array)
files.what: Same task, but a function `sort_it(n)` reads the array into heap memory, sorts it and returns the pointer. Descending order is printed by walking backwards.
steps: `sort_it` allocates `new int[n]`, reads values, and sorts ascending.
`main` prints the array forwards.
Then it prints it backwards for descending order.
`delete[] sorted_array` frees the memory.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: First line N, then N numbers.

check.q: Why must `sort_it` use `new` instead of a local array?
check.a: A local array would be destroyed when the function returns.

files.title: Sort It 2 (return a descending array)
files.what: A function reads the array into heap memory, sorts it in descending order with `greater<int>()`, and returns it to `main`.
steps: `main` reads `n` and calls `sort_it(n)`.
Inside: `new int[n]`, read, `sort(a, a+n, greater<int>())`, return `a`.
`main` prints and deletes it.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: First line N, then N numbers.

check.q: What is the return type of `sort_it`?
check.a: `int*` - a pointer to the first element of the heap array.

files.title: Monkey (sort letters of each line)
files.what: Reads lines until input ends, removes spaces, sorts each line's letters, and prints each line's sorted letters.
steps: `while (cin.getline(current_line, 100000))` reads every line.
Non-space characters are appended to the big buffer `all_lines_content`, and the line's start and length are remembered.
`sort(start, end)` sorts only that line's part of the buffer.
Finally each line's slice is printed.
files.complexity: Time O(L log L) per line · Space O(total length)
files.input_note: Several lines of lowercase letters and spaces.
files.output_note: `ekmnoy` (the letters of `monkey`, sorted) and `eefilloorvw` (`i love flower` with the spaces removed, sorted).
files.watch_out: The huge arrays (two `int[1000000]`, a `char[3000001]` and more) live inside `main`. That works here and on judges with a big stack, but on a default 1 MB stack it would crash; making them global (or `static`) is safer. A simpler solution: read each line into a `string`, drop spaces, `sort`, print. Also, `getline(current_line, 100000)` can't read a full 10^5-character line plus the null byte.

check.q: Why does this program crash on Windows?
check.a: Its local arrays need about 11 MB, but the default stack is about 1 MB (and 8 MB on Linux).

files.title: Who Is It? (best of three students)
files.what: For each test, reads three students and keeps the one with the highest marks, breaking ties by the smaller ID.
steps: Read three lines and build `s1`, `s2`, `s3` with the constructor.
Start with `best = s1`.
Replace `best` if another student has more marks, or equal marks and a smaller ID.
Save a heap copy of `best` in `students[i]`; print all at the end and delete them.
files.input:
2
1 sakib A 50
2 rakib D 96
3 akib C 96
1 tuli B 70
2 moni C 85
3 rina A 85
files.input_note: T, then 3 lines per test: ID name section marks.
files.output_note: Test 1: rakib and akib tie at 96, so the smaller ID `2 rakib D 96` wins. Test 2: moni and rina tie at 85, so `2 moni C 85`.
files.watch_out: `students[100]` is too small: T can be 1000. Use a larger array, or simply print the answer inside the loop.

check.q: What condition handles the tie rule?

files.title: Choose Three (brute force)
files.what: Tries every triple of different indices and says YES if any sums to S.
steps: Read `N`, `S` and the array.
Three nested loops `i`, `j`, `k` over all indices.
Skip triples where any two indices are equal.
If `A[i]+A[j]+A[k] == S`, the answer is YES.
Store answers and print them at the end.
files.complexity: Time O(N^3) per test · Space O(N)
files.input_note: T; then for each test `N S` and the array.
files.output_note: `YES` (for example 1 + 4 + 5 = 10), `YES` (2+2+2 = 6), `NO` (no three of 2, 8, 1, 5 add up to 4).
files.watch_out: `string results[100000]` inside `main` uses a few MB of stack. It runs here (and on judges with a big stack), but on a default 1 MB stack it would crash. T is at most 100, so `string results[100]` (or printing inside the loop) is enough. The inner loops also reuse the name `i`, which is legal but confusing.

check.q: How can you make the triple loop faster without changing the answer?
check.a: Start `j` at `i+1` and `k` at `j+1`, so each triple is checked once and the `!=` checks disappear.

recap: Heap arrays can be returned from functions; stack arrays cannot.
Tie rules: compare the first key, then the second.
Brute force is fine for small N - check the limits.
Keep huge arrays out of `main`'s stack.

check_yourself.q: Where should an array of a few million elements be declared?
check_yourself.a: As a global/static array or on the heap, not as a local variable.

check_yourself.q: How many triples does the brute force check for N = 100 with the full triple loop?
Name two ways to print an array in descending order after an ascending sort.
check_yourself.a: Loop from the last index to the first, or sort again with `greater<int>()`.

body: Nothing on this page is new. The mid-term takes the four tools of the first three modules and asks you to pick the right one under time pressure, so the useful revision is not "what does `sort` do" but "which question does each tool answer".
Here is the whole toolbox so far, written as questions rather than as names:
intro.trace:
the question you are asked     the tool for it
------------------------------------------------
read and print values          cin >>  /  cout <<
read a whole line with spaces  cin.getline(buf, N)
put values in order            sort(a, a + n)
biggest first                  sort(..., greater<int>())
order only part of a buffer    sort(a + l, a + r)
size known only while running  int* a = new int[n];
give that array back to main   return the pointer
keep several facts about
  one person together          class + constructor

body: The exam leans hardest on sorting, so do this one by hand before you read further. Take the five numbers `2 4 6 1 3` and the task: print them small to big, then big to small.

You read them into an array, call `sort` once, and print. For the second line you have a free choice: walk the same sorted array from the last index down to the first, or sort it again with `greater<int>()`. Both give the same line, and neither is more correct than the other.
intro.trace:
after reading        2  4  6  1  3
sort(a, a + n)       1  2  3  4  6
printed backwards    6  4  3  2  1

body: Two details of `sort` come back in the exam. The two arguments are a **start** and a **one-past-the-end**, so `sort(a, a + n)` means "indices 0 to n-1". Change those two and you sort a slice: `sort(a + 3, a + 7)` touches only indices 3, 4, 5 and 6 and leaves the rest of the array alone. That is how one long buffer holding several lines of letters can be sorted line by line.
And `sort` is not only for numbers. Characters are numbers, so sorting a run of letters puts them in alphabetical order: `monkey` becomes `ekmnoy`.
intro.snippet:
char b[] = "monkey";
sort(b, b + 6);      // b is now "ekmnoy"

body: The other half of the exam is about **where things live**. A function cannot return a local array, because the array dies when the function ends; it can return `new int[n]`, because heap memory stays until you `delete[]` it. That is the one reason those solutions use `new`.

The same question decides whether a program runs at all. A `int[1000000]` declared inside `main` asks for about 4 MB of stack, and the default stack on Windows is about 1 MB, so the program crashes before doing anything wrong. Declared above `main`, or as `static`, or taken with `new`, the same array is fine. Two programs below are logically correct and still crash for exactly this reason.

A class is the third tool, and it earns its place when one thing has several facts: an ID, a name, a section and a mark belong to one student, so they travel together in one object. Then a tie rule is one condition read left to right - compare the marks first, and only when they are equal look at the IDs.

Last, one habit worth carrying into the exam: read the constraints before choosing a method. Checking every triple of an array is three nested loops, and with N = 100 that is 100 x 100 x 100 = 1,000,000 checks, which finishes in no time. With N = 100000 the same loops would never finish. Brute force is not wrong; it is right or wrong depending on the limits printed in the statement.
The programs below are the exam solutions, each with its input, its output and the mistake it teaches.
